newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Feb 4.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Feb 4.

text.p: THE DOMINION

Australia wants to increase to two years the time New Zealanders have to wait before they can claim government benefits. New Zealanders living in Australia can claim benefits after six months' residence. Australians living in New Zealand can do the same under a reciprocal agreement. However, the Foreign Affairs and Trade Ministry's briefing paper to the Coalition Government says Australia has proposed amending the social security agreement "motivated by changes in Australian social policy and pressure on the Australian budget". Page 1.

The government has still not decided whether it will fund Aotearoa Television, and it refused to comment on the issue on Monday. A preliminary inquiry into the television station by unnamed contacts of Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters has been done and Peters briefed Prime Minister Jim Bolger before the Cabinet on Monday on its findings. Page 1.

An occasional "muffed pass" such as the Aotearoa Television Network funding issue should not do longterm damage to the National-NZ First coalition, National Party president Geoff Thompson said on Monday night. Speaking at a three-day National caucus meeting in West Auckland, Thompson said the coalition would learn from issues such as its handling of extra funding for the Maori TV company, and an earlier disagreement over the sale of minor lines off the Trans Power national grid. Page 2.

Women's Affairs Minister Christine Fletcher has promised strong action to "restore the place of the family", blaming years of change for putting the unit under threat. In her first policy statement in the role, she said she would initiate moves on behalf of women in diverse areas ranging from pay equity to representation "at the tables of power". Page 2.

Health Minister Bill English says it is up to the person who heads the independent inquiry into the safety of patients at Christchurch Hospital whether it will be held in public. Senior doctors from Christchurch Hospital Medical Staff Association said on Sunday they were concerned the inquiry might not be conducted publicly after failing at the weekend to gain such an assurance from English. Page 2.

Te Tai Rawhiti MP Tuariki Delamere's rapid political rise continued yesterday when he was named chairman of the Cabinet's expenditure control and revenue committee. Delamere was one of three NZ First MPs named chair of a Cabinet committee by Prime Minister Jim Bolger. Page 2.

The government would consider a call by NZ First deputy leader Tau Henare for a change in its policy on East Timor, Foreign Minister Don McKinnon said on Monday. However, McKinnon also said that supporting a referendum in East Timor on independence from Indonesia, as called for by Henare, could hinder other moves to resolve the issue. Page 2.

A High Court decision has divided an estimated $600 million worth of future gas supply from Kapuni field in Taranaki between Fletcher Challenge interests and heavyweight mining partners Shell and Todd. Todd Petroleum Mining managing director Richard Tweedie said the decision, delivered on Monday, meant some competition in the gas industry "at last". He believed the case was the biggest test to date of section 27 of the Commerce Act on competition in the marketplace. Page 13.

A second-quarter earnings surge is expected to ensure that Rupert Murdoch's News Corp records a rise of about 12 percent in first half net earnings to about A$760 million (NZ$850 million) when it reports this week. The result, due to be issued on Thursday, is expected to be under-pinned by stronger results from the media giant's American television operations and 20th Century Fox films. The movie division will be boosted by the success of worldwide hit Independence Day. Page 13.

Nestle, the world's second largest icecream manufacturer, will set up an icecream division in New Zealand in the next few months if it fails to buy Tip Top from Heinz Wattie. Nestle will bring one of its own brands to the country to compete against Tip Top, incustray sources said on Monday. Page 13.

Germany has turned to New Zealand for inspiration to solve problems in its labour market, the New Zeland-German Business Association was told. Germany's Economics Minister, Gunter Rexrodt, said the German economy was experiencing the impact of enormous adjustment pressures caused by globalisation. Page 13.

Evergreen Forests reported a $195,000 bottom-line loss for the six months to December 31 but increased the value of its forest plantations by 24 percent. The result compared with a loss of #135,000 in the previous corresponding period. Revenue of $695,000 compared with $1.5 million previously. No tax was paid in either year. Page 13.

The legal pendulum may be swinging in favour of activist shareholders after recent Australian trends and the Court of Appeal's decision regarding Asian Properties, law firm Kensington Swan says in a news-letter. "Justice McKay's surprisingly liberal view on shareholder activism in his delivery of the court's judgment should act as a strong warning to company directors and secretaries in New Zealand," Kensington Swan says. Page 13.
THE NEW ZEALAND HERALD

Government inquiries into Aotearoa Television have so far found no evidence of wrongdoing, the Prime Minister, Jim Bolger, indicated on Monday. Bolger was briefed by his deputy, Winston Peters, on an unofficial inquiry the New Zealand First leader had conducted using his contacts in Auckland. The Prime Minister told the New Zealand Herald that Peters' information was "useful" and he even appeared to endorse the unorthodox inquiry.

Private and corporate gas consumers stand to be the eventual beneficiaries of Monday's long awaited Kapuni gas judgment. Justice Sir Ian Barker's decision has further weekened the market dominance held by Natural Gas Corporation in gas wholesale markets by arming mining companies Shell and Todd Petroleum Mining with substantial amounts of gas to sell. However, the industry believes an appeal is a virtual certainty.

Telecom is in line for futher profit downgrades by local analysts as slower economic activity bites. One broker has already adjusted its profit forecast for the March-year from NZ$770 million to a little over $730 million before abnormals. Others were understood to be contemplating revisions around $740 million, in what would be the second general broker downgrade in the current year.

The legal pendelum may be swinging in favour of activist shareholders following recent Australian trends and the Court of Appeal's decision regarding Asian Properties, law firm Kensington Swan says in a newsletter.

Evergreen Forests reported a $195,000 loss for the December half year on revenue of $895,000. That compared to $135,000 loss for the previous corresponding period, which was struck on revenue of $1.5 million. The company said that the lower revenue was because of a reduction of harvesting on the West Coast of the South Island. It was believed that better log prices could be obtained by allowing trees to grow.

The drilling of three offshore exploration wells in Western Australia in the next six to nine months offers significant upside for New Zealand Oil and Gass shreholders the company said on Monday. In a December quarterly report, the company secretary, Gordon Ward, said the group was well placed to find exploration costs from production revenue as stronger Ngatoro oil production and higher oil prices took effect.
